subsystems.name: Synthetic genetic alphabet
subsystems.role: the replacement letters that carry heredity instead of, or alongside, A-T and G-C.
parts: modified sugar-phosphate backbones (for example threose or hexitol nucleic acid)
unnatural base pairs that pair by shape rather than hydrogen bonding only

subsystems.name: Replication and transcription machinery
subsystems.role: enzymes that can copy and read the synthetic letters, which natural polymerases cannot.
parts: XNAzymes — synthetic polymers that catalyse reactions themselves

subsystems.name: Host chassis
subsystems.role: a cell that tolerates the extra chemistry and stays alive.
parts: metabolic pathway supplying the unnatural precursors

subsystems.name: Biocontainment system
subsystems.role: keeps the organism dependent on something only the lab supplies, so it cannot spread.
parts: a genetic firewall so its genes cannot recombine with wild organisms

subsystems.name: Task gene circuit
subsystems.role: the actual job, such as breaking down a pollutant.
parts: sensor and promoter that switch them on only in the presence of the target

buildSteps.title: Choose the chemistry
buildSteps.detail: Pick a backbone modification and base pair whose geometry still lets a polymerase read it reliably, and check it is not toxic to the host.

buildSteps.title: Synthesise the building blocks
buildSteps.detail: The unnatural nucleotide triphosphates are made by chemical synthesis, not extracted from cells, and must be pure enough for enzyme work.

buildSteps.title: Evolve the polymerases
buildSteps.detail: Starting from a natural enzyme, rounds of mutation and selection in tiny water-in-oil droplets are used to find variants that copy and transcribe the synthetic alphabet without making too many errors.

buildSteps.title: Write the task circuit
buildSteps.detail: Genes for the chosen job — for example an enzyme that breaks a chlorinated solvent — are assembled with a sensor that turns them on only when the pollutant is present.

buildSteps.title: Build the host
buildSteps.detail: The circuit, the transporters and the replication machinery are inserted into a fast-growing microbe, and the strain is passaged for many generations to confirm the alphabet is not lost.

buildSteps.title: Install the containment
buildSteps.detail: The strain is made to require an unnatural amino acid or nucleotide to survive, and kill switches are added, then escape frequency is measured.

buildSteps.title: Test in a sealed bioreactor
buildSteps.detail: Degradation rate, growth and containment are measured under realistic pollutant concentrations and temperatures, with all exhaust and waste filtered.

buildSteps.title: Qualify and regulate
buildSteps.detail: Containment performance is documented against biosafety rules, waste streams are treated, and only then is any scale-up considered.

prerequisites.why: several non-natural backbones and base pairs have been made and shown to pair predictably.
enzymes that copy several XNA backbones have been evolved in the lab, but fidelity and speed remain far below natural replication.

prerequisites.tech: Cells that stably maintain an expanded alphabet
prerequisites.why: bacteria carrying an extra base pair have been grown, but keeping it stable over many generations without losing it is still hard.

prerequisites.tech: Orthogonal genetic systems that cannot exchange genes with wild life
prerequisites.why: this is the core safety idea, and no system yet guarantees it under real environmental conditions.
industrial fermentation already provides the sealed vessels and waste handling such organisms would need.

pathway.milestone: lab demonstrations such as XNAzymes with catalytic ability and bacteria carrying a sixth, unnatural base pair
pathway.unlocks: proof that heredity and catalysis are not restricted to natural DNA.

pathway.milestone: organisms whose entire genome uses a synthetic alphabet and which cannot swap genes with natural microbes
pathway.unlocks: a genuine genetic firewall, the key safety property.

pathway.milestone: contained industrial strains for degrading pollutants in sealed tanks
pathway.unlocks: clean-up of contaminated water and soil without releasing engineered life.

pathway.milestone: carefully monitored in-place use, if containment is demonstrated to be effectively irreversible
pathway.unlocks: remediation of sites that cannot be dug up or pumped through a reactor — a step that should only follow decades of containment evidence.
